Salt pulls water out of cells. If you salt something and let it sit in a dry cold environment the moisture that is extracted will evaporate and you end up with meat that has a lower moisture and a salty flavor that has soaked into it over time. If you salt a fresh cut of meat and immediately cook it, you will be combatting the moisture. The salt will be actively be pulling water from the tissue as you cook it. It also hasn’t had time to soak deep into the meat.

Salted meat will taste more “juicy” because when you eat it, the salt flavor stimulates your taste buds. This is true even if it is very dry jerky.

I suspect that a lot of people are confusing the perceived “juiciness” and flavor of a steak with their own saliva outputs

I'll be one of those people to say I prefer salting immediately before searing. As much as salting ahead of time allows you to get a much more even sear, it also gives me a larger and tougher grey band. Even when I pause your video as you're eating them side by side, it seems that the grey band on your salted steak is visibly drier and thicker than the unsalted.

We always hear that salting ahead of time allows more moisture to be retained, as the water is pulled to the surface then seeps back into the muscle fibers. I wonder though...how much water is lost to evaporation that doesn't actually seep back into the meat? After trying steaks both ways so many times, I'm finding it harder and harder to believe the salted steak is actually retaining more moisture (especially immediately under the surface). We say that salted steak leaves less moisture on the cutting board as though it's evidence it's a juicier steak...but perhaps it didn't have as much moisture to release in the first place? Salting ahead of time certainly has its benefits, but nothing that some papertowels and salted butter can't fix.

Here is our procedure: 
1. Season and sear steaks the day before.
2. Finish them on low heat in an oven the day of the party,.
3. Pull them out and rest them for at least twenty minutes, or long enough that that the outer layer is no hotter than the center.
4. move them into a holding oven set at about 120° F.
5. Plate them with whatever else is going on the plates and placing them in a holding oven.
6. Send them out to guests.

Just finished watching and I'd like to add something else. You said that the salted steak retains juices. But that's also not correct. Salting draws out water from the steak.
